notes: Reconciled from coders A and B. Both coded two university-layer Academic Integrity Office pages; no school or computing policy found, course layer deferred. Neither coder coded the Canvas-module implementation items on the AI survey, ethics prompts and sample class activity, nor the links to external guides, which are in the page but give no content beyond titles. One A-only unit (the section title 'Discussing GenAI with Your Students') was dropped because the fetched text has only the title. A: Coder A. Only the first of the two guidance pages is AI-specific; tips page units outside AI (integrity tips) are coded when they bear on cheating or assessment. The Canvas module and linked guides are not in the fetched text. B: Only two university-level Academic Integrity Office pages were screened in; no school or computing policy found. Navigation text and link lists were skipped. Several fit_notes mark integrity-prevention tips (P99) and a deterrence-by-reporting tip that no type covers well.

documents.title: Artificial Intelligence in Education
documents.summary: The Academic Integrity Office hub on AI in education explains why AI literacy matters, defines it, and gives instructors a Canvas module and links to guides, events and consultations. It sets no use rule.
documents.stance_why: The page never says AI is banned or allowed; it says 'Teaching, learning and assessments all need to change', offers an AI literacy module so instructors can 'guide students in using GenAI tools ethically and responsibly for your course(s)', and links to a guide for 'Crafting Your GenAI Course Policy'. The decision stays with instructors, so the stance is delegates.

units.why: Says 'Teaching, learning and assessments all need to change' because of LLMs. It calls for assessment redesign in general terms, so it fits P35 only partly: no specific redesign is given. Informs, addressed to all.
units.anchor: Teaching, learning and assessments all need to change.
units.fit_note: Generic claim that teaching and assessment must change; no concrete redesign is specified. Also (second coder): General claim that assessment must change; no specific redesign is named.
units.resolution_why: A coded actor admin, modality should; B coded actor all, modality informs. 'Teaching, learning and assessments all need to change.' is a general claim that addresses no one in particular and issues no instruction, so actor all and modality informs (B). Type P35 and phase general agree.

units.why: States the page will 'keep the UC San Diego community up-to-date', a commitment to ongoing updating of guidance. It is closest to P54 (policy revisited) but it is a page of updates, not a policy review cycle.
units.anchor: This page will try to keep the UC San Diego community up-to-date
units.fit_note: Commitment to keep a guidance page current, not a formal review of a policy.
units.resolution_why: Only B coded this. The source says 'This page will try to keep the UC San Diego community up-to-date on all things related to artificial intelligence and academic integrity', a real commitment by the office to keep guidance current. Kept as P54 informs with B's fit_note.

units.why: Says GenAI tools 'can replace and augment human thinking' and 'hinder and accelerate learning', naming both benefits and risks. It states benefits, so P87, but it is balanced rather than only positive.
units.anchor: GenAI tools present both challenges and opportunities for education.
units.fit_note: Two-sided: names harms (replace thinking, hinder learning) as well as benefits. Also (second coder): Names opportunities together with challenges.
units.resolution_why: Both coders coded the same sentence (A anchored 'They can replace and augment human thinking', B the opening 'GenAI tools present both challenges and opportunities for education'); all codes agree. B's anchor kept because it names both sides.

units.why: Cites survey results that students are worried about critical thinking and that '47% believe its easier to cheat with the tools'. This is data about AI's effect on students, so P55 (evidence), informs.

units.fit_note: Survey of student attitudes rather than learning outcomes.
units.resolution_why: Only B coded this. The source reports that students '47% believe its easier to cheat with the tools', survey evidence the page uses as its rationale. Kept as informs, P55 with B's fit_note.

units.frag_end: ethically and responsibly for your course(s).
units.fit_note: States that no campus-sponsored AI literacy training exists and puts the task on instructors. Also (second coder): Notes campus lacks training and asks instructors to fill the gap.
units.resolution_why: Modality differed: A may, B should. The source says 'you can help educate students', permissive wording, so may (A). Actor, phase, type and stance agree.

units.resolution_why: Only B coded this. The page quotes Sid Dobrin: 'They need to be taught how to use these tools responsibly, effectively, and efficiently', placed as support for its AI-literacy argument. Kept as P44 informs.

documents.title: Top 10 Tips for Instructors
documents.summary: Ten integrity tips for instructors, mostly about building belonging, redesigning assessments, reminders, monitoring, evaluation and reporting. AI appears in the expectations tip, assessment redesign ideas and sample statement.
documents.stance_why: The tips set no AI stance of their own; they tell instructors to "Make Standards and Expectations Absolutely Clear" and craft their own "GenAI & AI Policy", while giving sample wording that bans tools doing students' work.

units.frag_start: Sure, you could just tell them

units.resolution_why: A coded phase before-course, unit_stance restrict; B coded course-start, neutral. The statement is groundwork for creating a class code ('It is critical when you do this that you first set the groundwork'), so before-course (A). It sets no AI position, so neutral (B).

P71 is the closer type (A); P81 is for the formal procedure. A's fit_note kept.
